title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed p. 862 (Night 199, continuing nights-198), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 199 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. King Shahramān, overjoyed at his son's recovery, spends the night with the two young men. In the morning, alone with the prince, Marzawān tells him the whole story: the girl he met is the Lady Budūr, daughter of King al-Ghayūr; he tells him all that befell her and how greatly she loves him, and that everything that passed between the prince and his father has passed between her and hers. He bids him take heart, promises to bring them together soon, and recites two lines on the friend who joins estranged companions like the pin of a pair of shears. Marzawān goes on encouraging and consoling him until he eats and drinks; his spirit and strength return, and, cheered with poems and tales, he is soon on his feet and asks for the bath, where the two of them wash. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ التَّاسِعَةُ وَالتِّسْعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-tāsiʿatu wa-al-tisʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the ninth and the ninety after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and ninety-ninth night,
sentences.n: al-tāsiʿa, “the ninth”, feminine to agree with layla; then wa-al-tisʿūna, “and the ninety”, and baʿda al-miʾa, “after the hundred”, as in the nights before. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْمَلِكَ شَهْرَمَانَ بَاتَ تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ عِنْدَ هُمَا مِنْ شِدَّةِ فَرْحَتِهِ بِشِفَاءِ وَلَدِهِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-malika Shahramāna bāta tilka al-laylata ʿindahumā min shiddati farḥatihi bi-shifāʾi waladihi
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-king Shahramān spent-the-night that the-night with-them-two, from (the) intensity (of) his-joy at-(the)-healing (of) his-son.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that King Shahramān spent that night with the two of them, so great was his joy at his son’s recovery.
sentences.n: Shahrazād opens the night by repeating the last words of the one before. The print sets السعيدان solid, al-saʿīdu and anna run together, and this time it splits ʿindahumā, “with the two of them”, into two words, عند هما; both spacings are kept: السعيدان is read as two words, عند هما as one. min shiddati, “from the intensity of”: min gives the cause. farḥa bi-, “joy at”: bi- marks what the joy is over. The ء of شفاء is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ وَانْصَرَفَ الْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ وَخَلَا مَرْزَوَانُ بِقَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ حَدَّثَهُ بِالْقِصَّةِ مِنْ أَوَّلِهَا إِلَى آخِرِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu wa-inṣarafa al-maliku Shahramānu wa-khalā Marzawānu bi-Qamari al-Zamāni ḥaddathahu bi-al-qiṣṣati min awwalihā ilā ākhirihā
sentences.l: So-when morninged the-morning, and-went-away the-king Shahramān, and-was-alone Marzawān with-Qamar al-Zamān, he-told-him the-story from its-first to its-last.
sentences.i: When morning came and King Shahramān had gone, Marzawān, alone with Qamar al-Zamān, told him the whole story from beginning to end.
sentences.n: aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu, “the morning dawned”, verb and subject from the same root, ṣ-b-ḥ. khalā bi-, “to be alone with (someone)”: bi- marks the companion. ḥaddatha bi-, Form II, “to tell (someone) of”: the verb takes bi- for what is told. The answer to lammā, ḥaddathahu, comes only after all three clauses, as a plain perfect with no fa- or wa-, the regular form. The shadda of حدّثه and the madda of آخرها are printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ اعْلَمْ أَنَّنِي أَعْرِفُ الَّتِي اجْتَمَعْتَ بِهَا وَاسْمُهَا السِّتُّ بُدُورُ بِنْتُ الْمَلِكِ الْغَيُورِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu iʿlam annanī aʿrifu allatī ijtamaʿta bihā wa-ismuhā al-Sittu Budūru bintu al-maliki al-Ghayūri
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him: Know that-I know the-one-(f.)-whom you-met with-her, and-her-name (is) the-Lady Budūr, daughter (of) the-king al-Ghayūr.
sentences.i: And he said to him, “Know that I know the girl you were with: her name is the Lady Budūr, daughter of King al-Ghayūr.”
sentences.n: annanī, “that I”, the longer form of annī with the nūn of protection; its shadda is printed. allatī ijtamaʿta bihā, “the one (f.) whom you met”: ijtamaʿa bi-, Form VIII, “to come together with, meet”, and Arabic repeats the person in a returning pronoun, bihā, “with her”. al-sitt, “the lady”, is the word of the spoken language for a woman of rank, set before her name as a title.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ حَدَّثَهُ بِمَاجَرَي لِلسَّيِّدَةِ بُدُورَ مِنَ الْأَوَّلِ إِلَى الْآخِرِ وَأَخْبَرَهُ بِفَرْطِ مَحَبَّتِهَا لَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma ḥaddathahu bi-mā jarā li-al-sayyidati Budūra mina al-awwali ilā al-ākhiri wa-akhbarahu bi-farṭi maḥabbatihā lahu
sentences.l: Then he-told-him of-what happened to-the-lady Budūr from the-first to the-last, and-informed-him of-(the)-excess (of) her-love for-him.
sentences.i: Then he told him all that had befallen the Lady Budūr, from first to last, and how passionately she loved him.
sentences.n: The print sets بما جرى solid, بماجري, and writes the verb with ي for ى; both are kept, and the word is read bi-mā jarā, “of what happened”. ḥaddatha bi- and akhbara bi-, “to tell of, inform of”: both verbs take bi- for the news. jarā li-, “to happen to”: li- marks the one it happens to. farṭ, “excess”, of a love beyond measure; lahu, “for him”, li- marking the one loved. The madda of الآخر is printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ جَمِيعُ مَا جَرَى لَكَ مَعَ أَبِيكَ جَرَى لَهَا مَعَ أَبِيهَا وَأَنْتَ مِنْ غَيْرِ شَكٍّ حَبِيبُهَا وَهِيَ حَبِيبَتُكَ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu jamīʿu mā jarā laka maʿa abīka jarā lahā maʿa abīhā wa-anta min ghayri shakkin ḥabībuhā wa-hiya ḥabībatuka
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him: All (of) what happened to-you with your-father happened to-her with her-father; and-you, without doubt, (are) her-beloved, and-she (is) your-beloved.
sentences.i: And he said to him, “Everything that has passed between you and your father has passed between her and hers; and beyond all doubt you are her beloved, and she is yours;
sentences.n: The two lovers’ stories are set side by side in matching clauses: mā jarā laka maʿa abīka / jarā lahā maʿa abīhā, and ḥabībuhā / ḥabībatuka. Each refused marriage and was shut away by an angry father. laka, lahā: li- marks the one it happened to. min ghayri shakkin, “without doubt”. Here jarā is written with ى both times; compare بماجري just before.

sentences.t: فَشُدَّ عَزْمَكَ وَقَوِّ قَلْبَكَ فَهَا أَنَا أُوصِلُكَ إِلَيْهَا وَأَجْمَعُ بَيْنَكَ وَبَيْنَهَا قَرِيبًا وَأَعْمَلُ مَعَكُمَا كَمَا قَالَ الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: fa-shudda ʿazmaka wa-qawwi qalbaka fa-hā anā ūṣiluka ilayhā wa-ajmaʿu baynaka wa-baynahā qarīban wa-aʿmalu maʿakumā ka-mā qāla al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: So-tighten your-resolve and-strengthen your-heart, for-here I (am): I-bring-you to-her and-I-join between-you and-between-her soon, and-I-do with-you-two as said the-poet:
sentences.i: So steel your resolve and take heart; for here I am to bring you to her, and soon I shall unite you with her, and do for you both as the poet said:
sentences.n: shudda, imperative of shadda, “to tighten, bind fast”; qawwi, imperative of qawwā, Form II, “to strengthen”, with its final weak letter dropped. Both shaddas are printed. fa-hā anā, “and here I am”: hā draws attention to the speaker, who promises at once to act. ūṣiluka, Form IV of waṣala, “to bring (someone) to”. jamaʿa bayna … wa-bayna, “to bring together”: Arabic repeats bayna before each party. qarīban, “soon”, an adverbial accusative. ʿamila maʿa, “to do for, deal with”: maʿa marks the ones the deed is done for. ka-mā, “as”: ka- compares.

sentences.t:
اِذَا صَدِيْق صَدَّ عَنْ اِلْفِهِ * وَلَمْ يَزَلْ فِي فَرْطِ اِعْرَاضِ
اَلَّفْتُ وَصْلًا بَيْنَ شَخْصَيْهِمَا * كَأَنَّنِي مِسْمَارُ مِقْرَاضِ
sentences.tr:
idhā ṣadīqun ṣadda ʿan ilfihi * wa-lam yazal fī farṭi iʿrāḍi
allaftu waṣlan bayna shakhṣayhimā * ka-annanī mismāru miqrāḍi
sentences.l:
When a-friend turns-away from his-companion * and-ceases not in (an) excess (of) aversion,
I-join a-union between their-two-persons * as-though-I (were the) pin (of) scissors.
sentences.i:
When a friend turns his back upon his intimate, * and still keeps up his cold disdain,
I bring the two of them together, * as the rivet holds the scissor-blades.”
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The rhyme falls on iʿrāḍi / miqrāḍi. The print leaves صديق without its tanwīn; the metre needs ṣadīqun, and it is read so. ilf, “intimate, familiar friend”, and allaftu, “I joined in friendship”, Form II, come from the same root, ʾ-l-f, a play on the word; the print gives اَلَّفْتُ a fatḥa but no hamza. idhā with a noun, ṣadīqun ṣadda, puts the subject before its verb, as poetry allows. The image is the pin of a pair of shears, which holds two blades together at the point where they meet. ka-annanī: ka- turns anna into “as though”. The hamza of كأنني is printed.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ مَرْزَوَانُ يُقَوِّي قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ وَيُشَجِّعُهُ وَيُسَلِّيهِ وَيَحُثُّهُ عَلَى الْأَكْلِ وَالشُّرْبِ حَتَّى أَكَلَ الطَّعَامَ وَشَرِبَ الشَّرَابَ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal Marzawānu yuqawwī Qamara al-Zamāni wa-yushajjiʿuhu wa-yusallīhi wa-yaḥuththuhu ʿalā al-akli wa-al-shurbi ḥattā akala al-ṭaʿāma wa-shariba al-sharāba
sentences.l: And-not ceased Marzawān strengthening Qamar al-Zamān and-encouraging-him and-consoling-him and-urging-him onto the-eating and-the-drinking, until he-ate the-food and-drank the-drink.
sentences.i: Marzawān went on strengthening Qamar al-Zamān, encouraging him, consoling him and urging him to eat and drink, until he ate and drank.
sentences.n: lam yazal, “he did not cease”, with an imperfect, “he kept on doing”: the same phrase the poet has just used. Three Form II verbs in a row, yuqawwī, yushajjiʿu, yusallī, “to strengthen, embolden, console”, each with its shadda printed, as is that of yaḥuththu; ḥaththa ʿalā, “to urge to”, takes ʿalā for what one is urged to. akala al-ṭaʿāma wa-shariba al-sharāba, “ate the food and drank the drink”: each verb with a noun of its own root.

sentences.t: وَرُدَّتْ رُوحُهُ إِلَيْهِ وَعَادَتْ إِلَيْهِ قُوَّتُهُ وَنَجَا مِمَّا كَانَ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: wa-ruddat rūḥuhu ilayhi wa-ʿādat ilayhi quwwatuhu wa-najā mimmā kāna fīhi
sentences.l: And-was-returned his-soul to-him, and-came-back to-him his-strength, and-he-escaped from-what he-was in-it.
sentences.i: His spirit was given back to him, his strength returned, and he was delivered from the state he had been in.
sentences.n: ruddat, passive of radda, “to give back”: the print has no shadda, and the word could also be read active, raddat, “(his soul) returned”, as the spoken language uses the verb; the passive is the Classical reading. rūḥ, “soul, spirit”, is here feminine, as it often is. The shadda of قوّته is printed. mimmā, min + mā, “from what”; mā kāna fīhi, “what he was in”, his sickness.

sentences.t: كُلُّ ذٰلِكَ وَمَرْزَوَانُ يُسَلِّيهِ بِالْأَشْعَارِ وَالْحِكَايَاتِ حَتَّى إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ وَقَفَ عَلَى حَيْلِهِ وَطَلَبَ أَنْ يَرُوحَ إِلَى الْحَمَّامِ
sentences.tr: kullu dhālika wa-Marzawānu yusallīhi bi-al-ashʿāri wa-al-ḥikāyāti ḥattā inna Qamara al-Zamāni waqafa ʿalā ḥaylihi wa-ṭalaba an yarūḥa ilā al-ḥammāmi
sentences.l: All that, and-Marzawān consoling-him with-the-poems and-the-tales, until indeed Qamar al-Zamān stood on his-strength and-asked that he-go to the-bath.
sentences.i: All the while Marzawān kept him cheerful with poems and stories, until Qamar al-Zamān was up on his feet again and asked to go to the bathhouse.
sentences.n: kullu dhālika wa-…, “all that, and Marzawān …”: a clause of state, “all the while that Marzawān …”. sallā bi-, “to cheer, divert with”: bi- marks the means. ḥattā inna, “until”: after ḥattā a new clause may open with inna. waqafa ʿalā ḥaylihi, “he stood on his strength”, is spoken Arabic for being on one’s feet and strong again; ḥayl, “strength, power”, is an old word (Lane gives it beside ḥawl) that lives on in this everyday phrase. rāḥa, “to go”, is likewise the everyday verb; an yarūḥa, subjunctive after an. al-ḥammām, the public bath, where a recovered invalid went to wash off his sickness.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَ مَرْزَوَانُ بِيَدِهِ وَدَخَلَا إِلَى الْحَمَّامِ فَغَسَلَا أَبْدَانَهُمَا وَتَنَظَّفَا
sentences.tr: fa-akhadha Marzawānu bi-yadihi wa-dakhalā ilā al-ḥammāmi fa-ghasalā abdānahumā wa-tanaẓẓafā
sentences.l: So-took Marzawān by-his-hand, and-they-two-entered into the-bath, and-they-two-washed their-two-bodies and-they-two-cleaned-themselves.
sentences.i: So Marzawān took him by the hand, and they went into the bathhouse, washed their bodies, and made themselves clean.
sentences.n: akhadha bi-yadihi, “he took (him) by his hand”: the verb takes bi- for the part laid hold of. The verbs now go into the dual, dakhalā, ghasalā, tanaẓẓafā, “the two of them”; abdānahumā, “their bodies”, is a plural with the dual suffix. dakhala ilā, “to go into”, a common pairing beside plain dakhala. tanaẓẓafa, Form V, “to clean oneself”; its shadda is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
